title: Was the PMRC censorship in disguise?
summary: Josh and Chuck examine the Parents Music Resource Center (PMRC), the 1985 group of Washington wives (including Tipper Gore) that pushed for explicit-lyric labeling of albums. They trace its origins in the Darling Nikki controversy, the Cincinnati PTA letter, the Home Audio Recording Act tape tax that the RIAA sought, the September 1985 Senate Commerce Committee hearing featuring Frank Zappa, Dee Snyder and John Denver, the "Filthy Fifteen" list, the resulting Parental Advisory stickers, and the censorship that followed, including arrests tied to 2 Live Crew and Nirvana's "Rape Me" title change. Also includes a listener mail segment about Greek and Italian cultural affinity.

entities.name: Raising PG Kids in an X-Rated Society

segments.title: Opening banter and PMRC overview
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the PMRC topic, the 1980s context, and the Tipper Gore Darling Nikki origin story.

segments.title: Origins: Cincinnati PTA and Tipper Gore's book
segments.summary: Discussion of Tipper Gore's book Raising PG Kids in an X-Rated Society, the Cincinnati school PTA letter to the RIAA asking for voluntary ratings, and the RIAA's reluctance. Mike Love's $5,000 donation to kick off the PMRC is mentioned.
topics: Raising PG Kids in an X-Rated Society

segments.title: Home Audio Recording Act and the tape tax
segments.summary: The cassette tape tax (Home Audio Recording Act, HR 11) that the recording industry sought, and how it connected to the Commerce Committee that would also hold the PMRC hearing. Kids' tape-copying habits are discussed.

segments.title: PMRC media blitz and record industry deal
segments.summary: Hosts correct themselves: the record industry might have fought harder without the tape tax. The PMRC's media campaign on Donahue, the Today Show and in editorials spurred state labeling bills. Nineteen record labels agreed to cooperate before the hearing.

segments.title: The Filthy Fifteen list
segments.summary: The PMRC's list of fifteen songs tagged with X, D/A, V, and O categories, with discussion of the songs and frequent misreadings of their lyrics, such as Twisted Sister's Under the Blade and Def Leppard's High 'n' Dry, and Cyndi Lauper's She Bop.
topics: rating categories X D/A V O

segments.title: Senate hearing and testimony
segments.summary: The September 1985 Senate Commerce Committee hearing with Frank Zappa, Dee Snyder, and John Denver. Zappa argued the censorship was parental-in-name but government-backed; Denver opposed the labeling; Pat Boone said majority-approved censorship fits the Constitution; Senator James Exon questioned the purpose.

segments.title: Aftermath: stickers, store policies and arrests
segments.summary: Parental Advisory stickers began appearing in March; 2 Live Crew's Banned in the USA was the first. Broward County sheriff's deputies threatened record store clerks, and performers were arrested in Georgia. Walmart and others pressured artists, and Nirvana's Rape Me was retitled.
topics: Bobby Brown and Gene Simmons arrests

segments.title: Legacy and normalization of explicit content
segments.summary: Hosts argue the PMRC's efforts led to normalization of explicit music rather than moral decline, and note the record industry is no longer the gatekeeper.

segments.title: Listener mail: Greeks and Italians
segments.summary: A listener named Nick Kantos writes in about the Greek and Italian cultural affinity phrase, following up on an Olive Oil episode remark.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts give contact information and sign off.
